by Squarespace Squarespace: share your passion with the world. Why is the sky blue? Which came first: orange the color or orange
the fruit? And why is C3PO afraid of everything? Like, who decided it was a good idea to teach a droid to experience fear? There are some questions that we ask ourselves,
either as kids, or adults, or both. They’re questions about weird, everyday
things, and they’re weird because most of us don’t know the answers to them offhand. But most of the time, those questions turn
out to be pretty answerable. Like, for the ones I just mentioned, the short
answers are: Because of the way photons interact with the
molecules in the atmosphere. ...the fruit;
And…uh…’cause that’s what George Lucas wanted. Maybe because 3PO’s a protocol droid, and
they need to be able to relate to humans. Though, he could stand to turn his fear settings
down a notch. Now, as you know, philosophers have a soft
spot for questions that can never be answered. Most of the time, these puzzles make for great thought experiments – tests of our skills in logic and argument. But there are some questions whose very lack
of an answer can be downright troubling. Unlike the occasional fluke of physics or bit of Star Wars trivia, there’s a part of us that really wants, or even needs to have an answer to these things. For the past month or so, we’ve been exploring
the philosophy of religion, and we’ve been doing it mainly from a theistic perspective, looking into arguments that justify belief in God. But one of the most persistent challenges to god’s existence is also the root of one of the most-asked, but least answerable, questions that we, as
thinking beings, face. Why is there evil? [Theme Music] Evil comes in many forms. And likewise, for philosophers, poses many problems, especially vis a vis the existence of god. First, there’s what’s known as the logical
problem of evil. Like all rational people, theists can’t help but acknowledge that the world is full of evil. And here, we’re understanding “evil” to be all manner of bad stuff – like, not just Hitler or Darth Vader or Moriarty. It’s everything that’s in the vast spectrum of badness, from stubbed toes to plagues and everything in between. Theists and atheists both agree that evil exists in this way. But they disagree about the next part. Many theists believe in an omniscient, omnipotent,
omnibenevolent God. But atheists argue that this creates a contradiction – a set of beliefs that can’t all be true at the same time. Because, evil is bad, right – whether it’s stubbed toes or genocide or paper cuts or epidemics? So, if there’s really an all-knowing God
out there, he knows about all the evil. He might even know about it before it happens. And if he’s all-powerful, he could stop
it. And if he’s all-good, then he would want
to stop it. And yet he doesn’t. The evil continues. Philosophically rational people shouldn’t
hold inconsistent beliefs, so atheists argue that you’re going to have to give something up – and the thing to give up is God. Some theists, however, take a different route.
They choose to give up one or more divine attributes. They argue that maybe God isn’t powerful
enough to stop evil, or maybe he’s not knowledgeable enough to
know about it, or maybe he’s not even good enough to care
about stopping it. That might sound weird to some of you, but if you’ve ever heard someone say that
God is envious, or petty, or jealous, that’s basically what they’re doing – they’re acknowledging the possibility that
God is not actually good. If you’ve ever checked out the Old Testament, there is a God there who has some anger issues – one who’s not at all opposed to wiping out entire populations just because of some bad behavior. Still, despite this scriptural evidence, many
theists are committed to God’s omni-attributes, and are thus stuck with a problem. They
have to resolve the logical problem of evil and find some way to explain why God would
allow evil into the world. And if you can do that, then you are presenting
what is known as a theodicy. A theodicy is an attempt to show that the existence of evil doesn’t rule out the possibility of God’s existence. Yes, this is such a big deal that there’s
a word for it. And the most popular theodicy is called The
Free Will Defense. This argument holds that God maximized the
goodness in the world by creating free beings. And being free means that we have the choice to do evil things – a choice that some of us exercise. This theodicy says that God doesn’t create evil, but evil can’t be avoided without depriving us of our freedom. And a world without freedom would be a worse
place overall. This explanation preserves God’s goodness,
because he created the best possible world, and also preserves his omnipotence and omniscience,
because, although he does know about evil and could stop it, he has a good reason not to – to ensure our freedom. The problem is, the free will defense really only really addresses what’s known as moral evil – or the evil committed, on purpose, by humans. Now, we’re certainly responsible for a lot of bad stuff, but you can’t blame us for everything. We can’t be held responsible for the fact
that the plates of the earth sometimes shift, causing destructive earthquakes, or that a storm might knock a tree over that falls onto someone’s house. This type of evil – the stuff we’re not

###  Why is There Evil? 
This transcript explores the philosophical question of evil's existence. 

**Understanding Evil:** 
* It encompasses a wide range of bad experiences - from small inconveniences to global tragedies like genocide. 
* Theists and atheists agree on evil's existence, but disagree on God's role in it.

**The Logical Problem of Evil:** 
The question arises because both theists (believing in a God) and atheists (who don’t believe in God) acknowledge the reality of evil. 
* Theists: contend with its contradictions and the inability to reconcile God’s omnipotence with his alleged inaction against evil. 
  
**Theodicy:** 
It attempts to resolve the contradiction between a God who allows evils, a concept often called “why evil if God is all-powerful, omniscient & benevolent?” 
* The most common theodicy: “Free will Defense”. This argument states that God maximized good by allowing free will. Evil occurs as a side effect of having a choice to do good or bad, preserving freedom and God's goodness.

**The Free Will Defense vs Moral/Natural Evil:**   
The free will defense addresses “moral evil” -  intentional acts committed by humans, but not "natural evil"— events we don't have control over, like earthquakes or storms. 


**Religion Beyond Philosophical Thought:** 
Fiction can be a valuable way to address philosophical questions like the existence of God and evil in an unbiased manner.  The passage introduces Dostoevsky’s “Brothers Karamazov" as an example and provides insights about its role in navigating philosophy's intricacies.

**Overall Summary**: This  document explores the existence of evil, questioning how a benevolent being would allow it in a perfect world, offering "theodicy". It further discusses arguments on free will defense. The document also incorporates fictional narrative as an example, exploring how to deal with hypothetical situations philosophically and potentially challenge one's beliefs without taking sides in such debates.

The Problem of Evil

This podcast examines the philosophical challenge posed by the existence of evil. Despite recognizing evil's presence across diverse forms (from stubbed toes to genocide), believers face inconsistencies between their theological beliefs and observable examples of evil. The core debate centers on the relationship between divine attributes like omniscience, omnipotence, and omnibenevolence with the reality of earthly suffering. ### Contradictions in Belief The existence of evil raises important questions for both atheists and theists. * Atheists argue that an omnipotent, omniscient God should be able to stop all evil based on His ability to know about it prior, but choosing not to act is contradictory. * The belief in a God who allows evil while remaining fully good, creates a moral paradox - this is known as the “problem of evil”. ### The Theodicy Challenge Seeking resolutions, proponents of "theodicy" argue that the existence of evil doesn’t disprove the existence of God. A prominent argument is the "free will defense", emphasizing that allowing human beings free will allows for both good and bad choices. This defense posits that God created a world where individuals face such free-will decision options, some leading to harm, in order to ensure a morally meaningful world. ### Challenges and Solutions While the free-will defense focuses on moral evil, natural evil (like earthquakes or fallen trees) remains unresolved via this logic. It is important to note that people find personal interpretations of how God interacts with them through their beliefs - sometimes leading to philosophical debates as seen in Dostoevsky's character Ivan who breaks from his faith due to a strong ethical and spiritual conflict over accepting a God that allows evil. This summary presents complex philosophical themes, utilizing literature and real-world examples to delve into the enduring mystery of evil and God's place in humanity.

They argue that maybe God isn’t powerful enough to stop evil, or maybe he’s not knowledgeable enough to know about it, or maybe he has simply decided not to intervene.  The problem of evil is complex and difficult for philosophers and theologians alike. 

We'll now be exploring another important philosophical issue: the nature of evil. The free will defense really only addresses what's known as moral evil – or the evil committed on purpose by humans. In the novel "The Brothers Karamozov," 19th century Russian writer Fyodor Dostoevsky presents us with Ivan, who claims to believe in God. But Ivan finds the fact that God allows evil to exist to be so unforgivable that he decides worshipping such a God would be, just, unconscionable. Ivan goes as far as to declare that he is “returning his ticket” to heaven. If the same God who allows evil – particularly the suffering and death of children - is also saving a cozy place in paradise for Ivan, well, Ivan wants nothing to do with it. So, his way out of the problem of evil is to deny God’s goodness (and) conclude that a bad God isn't just unworthy of his worship; he’s not someone Ivan  wants to spend eternity with. It’s like the ultimate un-friending. Now, some readers have found Ivan's decision to be noble and full of integrity. After all, if you really think God is letting all of this bad stuff happen, why would you want to be on his team? But other people think Ivan is being irrational — why condemn yourself to eternity in hell on principle? For theists, it’s another question that doesn't have an easy answer. Thanks, Thought Bubble! Now, unlike Ivan, a lot of people aren't willing to give up their ticket to heaven. So they need to work on a way to keeping believing in and worshipping God even though evil is still a thing.

Religious beliefs regarding evil and its justifications  present contrasting viewpoints. Theists generally accept the existence of evil in a way that is shaped by God's attributes, such as omnipotence and omniscience. These attributes are considered core tenets of their religious belief systems.

Atheists posit potential contradictions within the notion of an omnipotent God who allows evil to exist, arguing for a fundamental issue with these attributes. The inconsistency arises from believing in a God that knows about everything, yet doesn't intervene in preventing bad events.  Philosophically speaking, this challenges the very nature of belief and can necessitate altering initial stances. 

Some theists take differing approaches. They consider limiting God's power by relinquishing beliefs like omnipotence or omniscience to appease this inherent conflict. Other theists focus on God not actively contributing to evil but accepting their own mortality and suffering.

Many theologians wrestle with 'Theodicy', a term describing an attempt to reconcile the presence of Evil. Free Will Defense, one prominent theory, posits that free will allows humans to choose bad actions while acknowledging good is maximized by God's intervention in this world. 

However, this defense struggles to explain natural evils stemming from natural phenomena that remain beyond human control. These events lack a clear link to intentional actions and fall outside the realm of moral responsibility. 

"Thought Bubbles", presented as fictional explorations of such scenarios, offer a different perspective on these complex points through narrative.  "The Brothers Karamozov's " Ivan,"  a character with devout religious beliefs, struggles to reconcile his faith with God's apparent inaction in allowing human suffering. Ivan attempts to sever ties from such an unsatisfactory existence and ultimately renounces belief in this god's benevolence, finding a place for personal freedom with self-imposed choices that align with a moral framework.

Hick's Soul-Making theodicy proposes a unique viewpoint where God intentionally imbues humans with imperfections in life. Theists and atheists both agree that evil exists in this way. But they disagree about the next part. Many theists believe in an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God. However, atheists argue that this creates a contradiction — a set of beliefs that can’t all be true at the same time. Because evil is bad, right — whether it’s stubbed toes or genocide or paper cuts or epidemics? So, if there's really an omniscient God out there, he knows about all the evil. He might even know about it before it happens. And if he’s all-powerful, he could stop it.  And if he’s all-good, then he would want to stop it. Yet, he doesn’t. Philosophically rational people shouldn't hold inconsistent beliefs; therefore, atheists argue you're going to have to give something up—and the thing to give up is God. Some theists, however, take a different route. They choose to give up one or more divine attributes.  They argue that maybe God isn't powerful enough to stop evil, or maybe he’s not knowledgeable enough to know about it, or maybe he's not even good enough to care about stopping it. That might sound weird to some of you, but if you’ve ever heard someone say that God is envious, petty, or jealous, that’s basically what they’re implying — they’re acknowledging the possibility that God isn’t actually good. If you've ever checked out the Old Testament, there is a God there who has some anger issues – one who’s not at all opposed to wiping out entire populations just because of some bad behavior. Still, despite this scriptural evidence, many theists are committed to God’s omni-attributes and are thus stuck with a problem. They have to resolve the logical problem of evil and find some way to explain why God would allow evil into the world. And if you can do that, then you're presenting what is known as a theodicy. A theodicy is an attempt to reconcile free will and a divine plan for human existence while explaining the continued presence of evil in the world. 

  Many theories about how this happens. Some are philosophical, some religious, and some based on personal beliefs. For instance:

* **Soul-making Theodicy:** John Hick argued that God deliberately creates us “unfinished” and our earthly lives are designed to toughen us up, kind of like boot camp. 
**Free Will Defense**: It argues that humans must be given freedom so they can exercise moral choice in the way God had planned for them (i.e., making a "good" choice) while accepting the responsibility for their choices or perhaps God's ultimate control over these choices.  


Some people believe this to be necessary for achieving true free will.

Overall, finding ways to reconcile suffering and evil with humanity’s faith in goodness often comes from deep philosophical reflection. The very act of engaging with these issues is a way to explore these problems and find personal meaning.

A discussion on theodicy was initiated from analyzing potential contradictions between God's existence and evil. It began with exploring how some theists struggle to reconcile the concept of God as simultaneously omnipotent, omniscient, and benevolent with the occurrence of evil in a world where he is described as angry with destructive capabilities, exemplified in the Old Testament. 

Theodicy attempts to address this philosophical problem by providing logical justifications for the existence of evil alongside the existence of good. The most prominent example is "the free will defense", which proposes that God designed humans as free beings capable of both good and bad choices in his creation, allowing for a world without entirely avoiding evil. While some find this explanation satisfactory, it only focuses on moral evil - the intentional actions of humankind.  

The debate was expanded to include natural evils, instances where external factors cause negative outcomes beyond human control (like natural disasters) for which free will defense offers no solution. A popular example is the Dostoevsky narrative and its protagonist Ivan's decision to "return his ticket" to heaven. Some interpret it as a philosophical display of integrity, while others view it as irrational. 

To address the problem of evil in the context of worshiping God, thinkers present various arguments. One of these proposes that the presence of both good and evil are inherently interconnected; without the opposing force of an opposite entity. Thus, understanding true goodness demands a complete picture encompassing both its existence and absence on equal ground. 

A different theodicy explored is Soul-Making theodicy as a counterpoint to the idea of God creating a perfect world that humanity ruins through choices; it suggests God intends for us to mature by being immersed in an imperfect environment of life's challenges. This process builds resilience and strong character which wouldn’t be possible with an entirely controlled or "safe" environment, according to proponents of this theodicy. 

While various solutions are proposed –  the difficulty lies in explaining why there remains so much evil in the world despite God's stated qualities and human efforts for positive endeavors. The question arises about if a level of necessary evil is necessary to establish understanding of goodness; would a minimal amount, such as injuries or everyday hardships, suffice instead of catastrophic suffering?

We don’t know what it feels like to be warm if we haven’t been cold. We can't understand the goodness of filling our bellies if we have never been hungry… However, there's also another way, though it involves a little more work on your part.  20th-century English philosopher of religion John Hick offered what's known as the soul-making theodicy. Unlike the traditional view that God created a perfect world which we ruined through our own poor choices, Hick argued that God deliberately creates us "unfinished" and our earthly lives are designed to toughen us up, kinda like boot camp. The harshness of life, Hick said, gives us a robust texture and character that wouldn’t be possible without an imperfect world. Hick said that we're not just God's little pets, and he's not our benevolent owner whose sole job is to keep us in a safe, comfortable environment. Instead, he wants to build us up – a strong foundation on this earth, preparing us for a journey that takes place beyond physical limitations in an eternal realm."

  “A lot of people have found a theodicy that satisfies them – one they believe reconciles the apparent evil in the world with God’s existence. Others find all of these theodicies to be flawed, and they reject God's omni-nature in favor of something less godlier.” While others are convinced that the evil in the world is simply incompatible with the existence of a god worthy of worship." 

Wherever you end up, this is a problem that needs to be grappled with. And you’ll probably be thinking about it long after this lesson has ended.  After all, today we've considered the biggest problem in theism – the problem of evil. We’ve thought  about different theodicies— or ways we might reconcile the existence of evil and the existence of God - and we've explored whether those responses are sufficient.
